title: What Limits Cross-Task Generalization in World Action Models?

paper.title: What Limits Cross-Task Generalization in World Action Models?
paper.abstract: Abstract Cross-task generalization remains difficult for world action models (WAMs), even when their predicted futures depict plausible manipulation. This gap can be attributed directly: we make this gap directly testable by decoupling a WAM into a world model and an inverse-dynamics model (IDM), then holding the IDM fixed while replacing the source of future images. We introduce Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE), a camera-space inverse-dynamics model pretrained on large-scale robot data, which provides this recovery interface for different future sources across tasks and environments. Through it, we find that actions recovered from recorded futures of unseen tasks execute almost as well as replayed demonstrations, whereas futures predicted by world models collapse across benchmarks. The failures are not generic: they concentrate on the gripper and interaction geometry while generation capacity is spent on task-irrelevant background. This diagnosis suggests that supervision should target exactly these regions. We therefore introduce the vision-to-action (VITA) loss, which passes generated futures through the frozen AoE and penalizes discrepancies in the recovered actions, redirecting generation toward action-relevant detail. Across two world models and three manipulation benchmarks, this simple change raises the execution success of generated futures from near zero to 47.0%. The same loss also transfers to WAMs and yields consistent gains in native control.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: World action models (WAMs) offer a compelling premise for embodied tasks: use the generalization capabilities of world models (WMs) to imagine future scenes, then condition an action head on the latent representations of those imagined futures to generate actions ( Li et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . This approach achieves strong performance on in-distribution tasks and under modest distribution shifts, yet falls substantially behind in more challenging settings, such as generalization across environments or tasks. This gap is often attributed to the difficulty of predicting 3D poses or to action heads that are tightly coupled to the environment encountered during training. Recent studies have also identified problems in world model predictions of robotic scenes, including physically implausible behavior and 2D-like flat appearance ( Shang et al., 2026 ; Co et al., 2026 ) . However, these analyses remain confined to 2D future videos that cannot be executed directly, leaving the impact of world model predictions on downstream cross-task generalization unquantified. Evaluating these videos through an inverse dynamics model (IDM) can also be inconclusive: exposure to trajectories from downstream environments during training may allow the IDM to compensate for distorted predictions, obscuring whether the predicted futures themselves support execution. To better evaluate the executability of future videos predicted by world models, we develop Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE). Pretrained on 9,637h of robot data, AoE uses camera-space representation to decouple action prediction from downstream environments. With little data from a downstream environment, AoE translates 2D gripper displacements and depth changes into executable poses. Figure 1: Overview of Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE) . Trained on 9,637 hours of robot image–action pairs, AoE infers the action between any two frames, serving as a bridge from video to action. Left: AoE enables evaluation of WMs: dreamed task completions in unseen environments are decoded into executable actions and assessed in the real environment. Right: The proposed vision-to-action (VITA) loss further improves the world (action) model by aligning actions recorded and inferred from dreamed and recorded videos. This enables interactive execution beyond the environments seen during pretraining, while keeping action trajectories out of training. On the same unseen benchmarks, we observe a substantial gap between recorded videos and world model predictions: actions recovered from recorded videos approach the success rate of replaying recorded actions, whereas those recovered from predicted future videos perform poorly. 2D flat appearance, physically implausible pose, and hallucinated scene substantially degrade the quality of the recovered poses ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Mi et al., 2026 ) . To address this limitation, we introduce the vision-to-action (VITA) loss, which uses AoE as a frozen supervisor to guide world models toward preserving the visual details needed for physically accurate gripper motion. We pass predicted future videos through AoE and use discrepancies of action-space representation to supervise action-relevant visual details ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . AoE’s sensitivity to gripper motion directs this supervision toward regions that matter for downstream execution ( Wi et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2020 ) . Gradients propagate through AoE to the world model while AoE itself remains frozen. VITA is natively suitable for world action model training to supervise predicted visual futures, allowing action-grounded visual supervision to shape the representations used for native action prediction. This supervision is applied during training and does not require the model to explicitly generate future images during execution. Our experiments examine three aspects of this approach. First, we use AoE to evaluate the cross-task executability of future videos generated by existing world models. Comparing generated futures with recorded videos reveals a substantial execution gap, highlighting a limitation in the transfer of world-model predictions to unseen tasks. Second, we evaluate VITA in both world models and world action models. VITA substantially improves the execution success of actions recovered from generated futures and improves native action prediction in LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026a ) and FastWAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , with particularly pronounced gains under distribution shifts ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Zhen et al., 2026 ) . FastWAM benefits even though it does not explicitly generate future images during inference. Third, we study how scaling AoE’s pretraining data affects its roles as both an evaluator and a supervisor. Larger-scale pretraining improves action recovery on unseen tasks and yields stronger downstream performance when the frozen AoE is used for VITA supervision. Our contributions are threefold: (1) we introduce AoE, an inverse dynamics model that uses the camera-space action representation to support zero-shot cross-task generalization; (2) we propose VITA, an action-grounded loss that uses frozen AoE supervision to guide both WMs and WAMs to preserve visual details needed for executable 3D pose changes; and (3) we demonstrate that VITA raises the cross-task execution success of world-model-generated futures from near zero to 47.0% and improves native action generation in WAMs under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution.

sections.heading: Forward and inverse dynamics.
sections.text: Let o t o_{t} denote the robot’s observation at time t t , a t a_{t} its action, and ℓ \ell a language instruction specifying the task. A forward dynamics model (FDM) predicts the consequences of an action. Written in observation space, its prediction takes the form o ^ t + 1 = ℱ θ ​ ( o t , a t ) , \hat{o}_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(o_{t},a_{t}), (1) where θ \theta denotes the model parameters and o ^ t + 1 \hat{o}_{t+1} is the predicted next observation. An inverse dynamics model (IDM) infers an action consistent with an observed transition: a ^ t = 𝒟 ϕ ​ ( o t , o t + 1 ) , \hat{a}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{\phi}(o_{t},o_{t+1}), (2) where ϕ \phi denotes the IDM parameters. These two mappings connect actions and observations in complementary directions: forward dynamics predicts what an action will produce, while inverse dynamics recovers an action that could produce a given transition. Applied to selected frame pairs from a video, inverse dynamics provides a way to translate visual changes into robot actions.

sections.heading: From world models to world action models.
sections.text: In embodied tasks, a world model provides the visual-prediction component of a policy. An instruction-conditioned world model predicts a task-directed future observation from the current observation and instruction. WAMs integrate this prediction process with action generation ( Li et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . In attention-based architectures, an action head reads internal visual features associated with the predicted future. We summarize this interface as h t = ℋ θ ​ ( o t , ℓ ) , a ^ t = 𝒜 ψ ​ ( o t , ℓ , h t ) , h_{t}=\mathcal{H}_{\theta}(o_{t},\ell),\qquad\hat{a}_{t}=\mathcal{A}_{\psi}(o_{t},\ell,h_{t}), (3) where h t h_{t} denotes the latent features associated with future prediction, ℋ θ \mathcal{H}_{\theta} denotes their computation within the world model, and 𝒜 ψ \mathcal{A}_{\psi} is the action head. Attention allows the action head to access h t h_{t} during action prediction. Training this coupled system on downstream data ties the visual features to the action head that consumes them. Future imagination therefore influences control through an internal representation, and task success reflects the behavior of the combined system. This makes it difficult to directly assess how the predicted visual future itself supports execution on unseen tasks. We introduce an explicit image-space interface between future prediction and action recovery: o ^ t + 1 = 𝒲 θ ​ ( o t , ℓ ) , a ^ t = 𝒟 ϕ ​ ( o t , o ^ t + 1 ) , \hat{o}_{t+1}=\mathcal{W}_{\theta}(o_{t},\ell),\qquad\hat{a}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{\phi}(o_{t},\hat{o}_{t+1}), (4) where 𝒲 θ \mathcal{W}_{\theta} is the instruction-conditioned world model and 𝒟 ϕ \mathcal{D}_{\phi} is an independently pretrained IDM. We first evaluate the IDM on recorded transitions from unseen tasks. We then replace the recorded future observations with world-model predictions while keeping the IDM frozen. This shared action-recovery interface allows us to evaluate IDM transfer and the executability of generated futures separately under the same execution protocol.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We introduce AoE, an inverse dynamics model pretrained on 9,637 hours of robot image–action pairs, and use it as a frozen interface for evaluating and improving WMs and WAMs for embodied tasks. Section 3.1 presents AoE’s overview and our protocol for evaluating the executability of future videos generated for unseen tasks. Section 3.2 introduces the AoE-based vision-to-action (VITA) loss and its integration into world-model and WAM training. Section 3.3 analyzes how this loss guides future prediction and improves downstream execution. Figure 2: Cross-task generalization evaluation and the VITA loss. Left: Future videos generated by the WM in unseen environments are fed into AoE frame-by-frame to obtain camera-space representations, which are translated into 3D poses and executed in the real environment for evaluation. Middle: Dreamed future frames are decoded by AoE into actions, and the WM is updated by minimizing their discrepancies against actions inferred from recorded videos as well as the ground-truth actions. Right: The vision-to-action loss is transferred to WAM. By encouraging the future video to focus on task-critical regions, the native action generation of WAM is improved under cross-task generalization.

sections.heading: 3.1 Camera-Space Inverse Dynamics for Cross-Task Evaluation
sections.text: An IDM infers actions that connect a current observation o t o_{t} to a future observation o t + i o_{t+i} . Predicting pose-based actions directly in environment coordinates ties this mapping to the coordinate convention of the training environment: the same end-effector motion can correspond to different action values under different world or robot-base frames. The action head consequently learns both the motion implied by the images and an environment-specific coordinate mapping. We separate these two operations with a camera-space action representation. For arm r ∈ { ℒ , ℛ } r\in\{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R}\} , AoE predicts a ^ t , t + i r = 𝒟 ϕ r ​ ( o t , o t + i , s t ) ∈ ℝ d a , \hat{a}^{\,r}_{t,t+i}=\mathcal{D}^{r}_{\phi}(o_{t},o_{t+i};s_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}, (5) where s t s_{t} is the current robot state, and d a d_{a} denotes the dimension of the camera-space action target. AoE summarizes each arm’s motion a ^ t , t + i r \hat{a}^{\,r}_{t,t+i} by its projected start and end positions, relative depth change, orientation change, and gripper command from timestamp t t to t + i t+i . This compact target captures the transition between the two observations and provides a common prediction space across environments. The target encoding and its conversion into executable poses using camera calibration are specified in Appendix B ; the complete architecture and token routing are given in Appendix C . Through large-scale pretraining on robot interaction data, AoE learns to recover end-effector motion from paired observations in this shared representation. Environment-specific coordinate conversion is handled explicitly at execution, allowing the learned image-to-action mapping to be reused across downstream environments. AoE remains frozen after pretraining.

sections.heading: Evaluating cross-task future videos.
sections.text: Given an initial observation and a task instruction, a WM generates a sequence of future observations. We apply AoE to consecutive frame pairs, recover the corresponding pose commands, and execute them to measure task success. This turns predicted videos into an execution-based test of cross-task generalization. We first evaluate the same procedure on recorded videos from tasks excluded from AoE pretraining, establishing the action-recovery model’s transfer performance. We then substitute world-model predictions while keeping AoE, the initial conditions, and the execution protocol fixed. If the generated futures preserve the information needed for control and AoE reliably recovers the corresponding actions, this pipeline supports zero-shot execution on unseen tasks. The comparison with recorded videos measures how replacing genuine visual transitions with predicted ones affects downstream success.

sections.heading: 3.2 Vision-to-Action Future Supervision
sections.text: World-model video objectives treat visual content broadly, while downstream manipulation depends strongly on the relative geometry of the gripper and the target object. AoE provides an action-grounded training signal for this geometry. We use the pretrained AoE model as a frozen supervisor during world-model training, so that the generated future is evaluated according to the action information it conveys. Given the current observation o t o_{t} , let o t + i o_{t+i} denote the recorded future observation and let o ^ t + i \hat{o}_{t+i} denote the corresponding world-model prediction. We pass both observation pairs through AoE under the same robot state, noisy action, and flow time. Let f ϕ ​ ( o t , o ) f_{\phi}(o_{t},o) denote AoE’s action-flow prediction conditioned on the observation pair ( o t , o ) (o_{t},o) , and let 𝐯 t , i ⋆ \mathbf{v}^{\star}_{t,i} denote the ground-truth action-flow target. The core objectives are ℒ match = 𝔼 [ ‖ f ϕ ( o t , o ^ t + i ) − f ϕ ( o t , o t + i ) ‖ 2 2 ] , ℒ GT = 𝔼 [ ‖ f ϕ ( o t , o ^ t + i ) − 𝐯 ⋆ t , i ‖ 2 2 ] , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{match}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|f_{\phi}(o_{t},\hat{o}_{t+i})-f_{\phi}(o_{t},o_{t+i})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right],\quad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GT}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|f_{\phi}(o_{t},\hat{o}_{t+i})-\mathbf{v}^{\star}_{t,i}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (6) where the expectation averages over training transitions and the shared action-noising conditions. We refer to their sum, ℒ VITA = ℒ match + ℒ GT \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VITA}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{match}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GT}} , as the VITA loss. The matching term transfers action-relevant information from the recorded future, while the ground-truth (GT) term anchors this information to the action that produced the transition. We add ℒ VITA \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VITA}} to the native world-model objective during cross-task training. Gradients are propagated through the generated-image branch while AoE remains frozen, allowing the WM to improve the visual details that affect action recovery. The flow-target construction and implementation details are provided in Appendices D and I .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We conduct extensive experiments on both the decoupled WM + IDM architecture and WAMs, aiming to answer the following questions: Q1: Do world-model-generated future videos support execution on unseen tasks? (Section 4.1 ). Q2: Can the proposed VITA loss help world models achieve cross-task generalization, and can it transfer to WAMs, improving their native action inference? (Section 4.2 ). Q3: How does AoE’s pretraining data scale affect its roles as evaluator and teacher? (Section 4.3 ). Q4: How do AoE’s action representation and the components of VITA affect performance? (Section 4.4 ).

sections.heading: Setup.

For cross-task generalization, models are trained on the LIBERO-90 training split with the test tasks held out, and evaluated in the standard LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . sections.heading: 4.1 How Executable Are World Model Futures on Unseen Tasks?
sections.text: To evaluate the executability of world-model-generated future videos across tasks and environments, we generate future videos with Cosmos ( NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) and WAN2.2 ( Wan et al., 2025 ; Wan Team, 2025 ) from held-out initial observations and instructions, and recover actions with the frozen AoE. Table 1 shows that the evaluation itself is sound: on recorded videos, AoE recovers most of the replay performance, reaching 57.0% average success on LIBERO against 72.3% for replaying recorded actions, with RoboTwin following the same pattern. Generated futures, however, collapse. Both world models succeed on at most 0.4% of LIBERO trials under pass@1. The gap persists under cross-environment evaluation (Table 2 ), where recorded images still reach 47.0% overall on LIBERO-Plus while generated futures stay under 4%. Inspecting the failed generations reveals why: both models spend their capacity on task-irrelevant background, while the gripper is generated with flat appearance, physically implausible finger configurations, and hallucinated content that contradicts the observed scene, and these defects translate directly into erroneous recovered poses. sections.heading: Cross-task executability.
sections.text: We add the VITA loss of Section 3.2 to concentrate generation on action-relevant regions. Table 3 shows that this simple change makes generated futures executable: WAN2.2 reaches 47.0% average success on LIBERO and Cosmos 51.7%, approaching the 57.0% of recorded images, and RoboTwin Hard rises from around 1% to 40.4% and 36.4%, respectively. The gains persist across environments (Table 4 ), where both models reach about 30% overall on LIBERO-Plus. To test whether this improvement depends on using AoE as both the VITA teacher and the execution evaluator, we keep the same VITA-supervised WAN2.2 checkpoint and replace only the IDM used after video generation. We further evaluate VITA-trained futures with J-IDM ( Li et al., 2026b ) and the DreamGen IDM ( Jang et al., 2025 ) ; detailed results are reported in Appendix H .

sections.heading: VITA for world action models.
sections.text: Adding ℒ VITA \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VITA}} to LingBot-VA and FastWAM training improves both architectures in-distribution (Table 5 ); on RoboTwin, for example, LingBot-VA rises from 84.9% to 91.8% average success. The benefits are substantially larger out of distribution (Table 6 ): LingBot-VA improves from 35.1% to 47.2% overall on LIBERO-Plus, with the largest gains under background and lighting changes, and raises RoboTwin Hard success from 19.2% to 31.6%. FastWAM follows the same trend, which is notable because its inference path never renders future images, and the improvement arrives purely through training, as analyzed in Section 3.3 . sections.heading: 4.3 Scaling AoE Pretraining
sections.text: Both the evaluation and the supervision above rely on AoE, so we study how its pretraining data scale affects each role by partitioning the corpus into mini-sets and adding them successively, spanning 500 to 9,500 hours. As Figure 3 (left) shows, the gripper pixel error on held-out tasks drops from 12.6 px to 3.6 px while the zero-shot success rises from 1.7% to 57.0%. The converged VITA loss descends together with the pretrain loss across data scales (middle), remaining a well-behaved proxy as the teacher improves. Downstream (right), LingBot-VA’s LIBERO-Plus success with a frozen AoE grows monotonically with teacher quality and overtakes the no-VITA baseline between 3,500 and 5,000 hours, whereas a trainable AoE stays nearly flat. Since updating the teacher erodes the calibrated interface that makes the supervision meaningful, AoE remains frozen in all experiments.

sections.heading: Camera-space vs. 3D-pose actions.
sections.text: The 3D-pose variant fits its training environments better than AoE, but this fit comes from memorizing environment-specific coordinate conventions: it recovers executable actions on unseen tasks at 0.0% zero-shot and 2.3% with 10-shot adaptation, where the camera-space representation reaches 29.2% and 37.8% (Table 8 ). Because the camera-space target is defined by observable image geometry, the same action interface transfers across environments without relearning a task-specific world-frame mapping. Figure 4: VITA loss computed with different IDM variants. IDM is not suitable for updating with world models. 3D pose performs better, especially in environments with severe screen occlusion.

sections.heading: What does camera space cost without transfer?
sections.text: Figure 4 compares six IDM variants as VITA supervisors within a fixed environment. Pretraining matters more than the representation: from-scratch IDMs of either type supervise poorly, while a two-stage trained 3D-pose IDM is competitive. Weak supervision is worse than none: both from-scratch variants fall on LIBERO-Plus below the baseline trained without VITA, indicating that an uncalibrated teacher actively misdirects the world model. Adapting the IDM to the downstream environment in a second stage recovers much of this deficit, yet still lags large-scale pretraining on LIBERO-Plus, suggesting that per-environment adaptation alone does not match the supervision quality of a broadly pretrained teacher. 3D pose performs better because camera-space supervision becomes unreliable under severe occlusion. The camera-space pretrained AoE remains the best supervisor on LIBERO-Plus at 47.2%, and trails 3D-pose 2-stage only on RoboTwin Hard.

sections.heading: Why the matching loss.
sections.text: The GT loss alone reaches 45.5% on LIBERO-Plus but only 24.7% on RoboTwin Hard (Table 8 ). The reason is structural: when the gripper leaves the camera view or the camera undergoes deformation, camera-space GT targets become undefined and provide little signal. The matching loss transfers action-relevant information from the recorded future without requiring a pose estimate and further disambiguates multi-solution observations, so the full VITA objective performs best on both benchmarks.

sections.heading: Grounded world-model evaluation.
sections.text: A growing body of work evaluates world models in embodied scenarios. WorldArena jointly scores perceptual quality and functional utility, revealing a persistent gap between visual fidelity and embodied usefulness ( Shang et al., 2026 ) . KineBench grounds generated videos kinematically, extracting end-effector poses from individual frames for closed-loop execution and trajectory-level analysis ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , and WorldSimProbe issues controlled simulator queries to test action realization and interaction grounding ( Co et al., 2026 ) . Despite this progress, existing evaluations remain confined to imagination: they score the generated videos themselves, or execute them only through extractors tied to their training environments, leaving unquantified whether a predicted future can be carried into an unseen environment and actually executed ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . We therefore use dataset-image and recorded-action replay to calibrate IDM transfer, and hold the pretrained IDM fixed across visual-source replacements, human judgments, and local geometric interventions.

sections.heading: Video and inverse-dynamics priors for control.
sections.text: DreamGen converts generated videos into neural trajectories for policy training ( Jang et al., 2025 ) . LingBot-VA couples causal video modeling with action prediction ( Li et al., 2026a ) , while Fast-WAM studies video co-training under several inference interfaces ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) . VERA combines video planning with a Jacobian-based inverse dynamics model ( Li et al., 2026b ) . GE-Act 2.0 separately pretrains a visual planner and IDM, then jointly optimizes them through generated future states using action flow matching and compatibility-based selection ( AgiBot Research Team et al., 2026 ) . These approaches establish visual prediction and inverse dynamics as complementary components of robot learning. We evaluate a pretrained, frozen camera-space IDM through dataset-image replay on held-out tasks and transfer its action knowledge into future-image supervision.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Pretrained inverse dynamics provides a common action model for evaluating and supervising visual futures. We introduce AoE, an inverse-dynamics model built on a camera-projection action representation with zero-shot cross-task generalization, through which world-model futures are carried from video into interactive execution in the environment. Building on this interface, we further propose the VITA loss, which substantially improves the cross-task generalization of world models. We also extend VITA to world action models, obtaining consistent gains across multiple architectures and evaluation environments. Constrained by the camera-projection representation, AoE cannot handle tasks where the gripper leaves the camera view for extended periods or the camera is severely occluded, and would raise additional safety concerns in real-robot evaluation; we expect these limitations to be addressed in combination with future work on active exploration.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with checking the training and evaluation data pipelines and code, polishing the language of the manuscript, and developing and checking the mathematical derivations for the VITA loss. We have not used generative AI tools for any other tasks requiring disclosure, and the remaining required disclosure categories are not applicable to this work. sections.text: We provide detailed training and evaluation configurations in Appendix F , including the composition and proportions of the pretraining data in Appendix F.1 , and detailed experimental results in Appendix G . sections.heading: Appendix A Attention Maps and Camera-Space Representations on Seen and Unseen Tasks
sections.text: We visualize AoE on two types of data: a validation split sampled from the pretraining dataset and tasks from unseen environments. The same frozen AoE checkpoint is used in both cases.

sections.heading: Attention maps.
sections.text: Figure 5 shows attention maps for the validation split and unseen tasks. Across both settings, the attention is concentrated around the robot end effector and the object being manipulated, while receiving less emphasis from background regions. This behavior is consistent with the action-grounded sensitivity analyzed in Section 3.3 : visual changes near the end effector and the target object have a direct effect on the action-flow prediction. The attention maps provide a qualitative visualization of this behavior, while the formal analysis in Section 3.3 is based on the local sensitivity of AoE’s action-flow output to its visual input. Figure 5: Attention maps on seen and unseen tasks. AoE focuses primarily on the robot end effector and the object being manipulated in both the validation split and unseen environments.

sections.heading: Camera-space representations.
sections.text: Figure 6 visualizes the camera-space action representation predicted by AoE. The examples are obtained from recorded videos in the validation split and unseen environments. For each observation pair, AoE predicts the two-dimensional end-effector trajectory in the camera image, shown as the overlaid line between the recorded start and end frames. The plot below each example shows the corresponding predicted relative-depth change. These visualizations show that AoE produces a consistent camera-space representation across seen and unseen tasks, without requiring the action target to be expressed in a task-specific world coordinate frame. sections.heading: Execution from video.
sections.text: For a generated video, AoE processes consecutive frame pairs. At each execution step, the current robot state supplies the initial pose required for reconstruction. Camera calibration, action normalization, and controller conventions remain fixed when comparing recorded and generated videos. All coordinate conversions are deterministic, and AoE retains its pretrained parameters throughout evaluation.

sections.heading: Appendix C Inverse-dynamics architecture and protocol details
sections.text: Figure 7: The AoE inverse-dynamics architecture. Two independent image towers encode external-camera observations at the start and end of a transition. Alternating attention blocks connect shared visual features to two arm-action tokens. Direct state access is routed by arm; self-attention supports coordination. The output parameterizes translation in image coordinates and depth, with rotation and gripper control.

sections.heading: Visual and action streams.
sections.text: AoE receives two external-camera images, ext_start and ext_end . Each timestamp has an independent DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) ViT-L/16 encoder; both full encoder parameter sets are updated during AoE pretraining. Each encoder produces 201 tokens: one class token, four register tokens, and 196 patch tokens on a 14 × 14 14\times 14 grid. Learned view embeddings distinguish the timestamps, producing 402 visual conditioning tokens. The model uses no wrist-camera input (Figure 7 ). The 18-dimensional proprioceptive vector is split into two nine-dimensional arm states. A shared state MLP produces tokens s L s_{L} and s R s_{R} , bringing the conditioning stream to 404 tokens. The query stream has 34 tokens: 32 future-representation tokens and two 12-dimensional arm-action tokens projected into the transformer width. The action-token axis indexes arms. The transformer has width 1536, 16 layers, 32 attention heads of dimension 48, and MLP hidden width 1024, with approximately 450 million parameters. Together with both visual encoders, AoE contains approximately 1.14 billion parameters.

sections.heading: State routing and positional information.
sections.text: Even-indexed layers use cross-attention over the visual and state conditioning stream. The left action token attends to all visual tokens and s L s_{L} ; the right action token attends to all visual tokens and s R s_{R} . The 32 future tokens attend to the complete conditioning stream. Odd-indexed layers apply unmasked self-attention across queries, allowing information exchange and bimanual coordination. Thus, the cross-attention mask routes direct state access, while self-attention permits indirect cross-arm influence. Cross-attention uses two-dimensional axial rotary positional embeddings. Image patches carry their row and column coordinates, and each query token has a learned two-dimensional reference point. Both state tokens use coordinate ( 0 , 0 ) (0,0) . The arm-supervision mask expands across all 12 action coordinates. If a minibatch contains multiple temporal pairs k k , the numerator of the masked pretraining loss sums over ( b , k , r ) (b,k,r) and coordinates, and its denominator is 12 ​ max ⁡ ( 1 , ∑ b , k , r m b ​ k ​ r ) 12\max(1,\sum_{b,k,r}m_{bkr}) . The same reduction applies at every sampled flow time. Unsupervised arms receive no direct loss contribution.

sections.heading: C.1 Task splits and frozen-model reuse
sections.text: LIBERO source tasks are selected from LIBERO-90 after excluding evaluation-task identities. The exclusion is applied before AoE pretraining. Dataset image replay evaluates the pretrained checkpoint on recorded transitions from these unseen tasks. The world-model source comparison reuses the same checkpoint for recorded, cross-task generated, and VITA-supervised generated futures. The VITA condition updates the world model alone. RoboTwin uses two-fold task-level cross-validation with 25 training tasks and 25 held-out tasks per fold. The two groups exchange roles between folds. Each fold reuses its pretrained AoE checkpoint with frozen parameters. The complete task partition is given in Appendix F.4 . The native WAM transfer comparison trains on LIBERO-90 and evaluates the LIBERO Long, Goal, Object, and Spatial suites, with 500 episodes per suite and 2,000 episodes in total. The All training objectives in Table 20 share this split, including the native and DINO controls. The same-domain world-model comparison uses 500 episodes, with target adaptation supplied 50 demonstrations per task. Standard LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus native-control experiments use training on benchmark tasks and are reported as a separate evaluation setting. AoE parameters remain frozen after pretraining, except in the explicitly identified trainable-teacher scaling ablation in Section 4.3 . Source-validation data provide model selection and the offline confidence weights used by the auxiliary loss. Confidence calibration changes loss weights while preserving the pretrained model. In downstream WAM training, differentiation through AoE’s generated-image input transfers supervision to video and shared parameters. Each WAM uses its native action path for evaluation. The fold teacher and its confidence calibration are shared across downstream architecture comparisons.

sections.heading: C.2 Calibration protocol
sections.text: Held-out task calibration fixes task identities before evaluation and excludes their demonstrations from AoE pretraining. Recorded actions and future images share the simulator snapshot and temporal interval. Camera perturbations are applied when rendering both images of a pair. We report full-set performance, the coverage and performance of instances with successful recorded-action replay, and their subset with successful demonstration-image recovery. An independent geometric recovery pipeline repeats the source comparison and the paired visual interventions. Rotation targets encode the start-to-end relative rotation in a consistent reference frame, and depth normalization is inverted before Eq. ( 19 ). Appendix I specifies the complete auxiliary training objective, confidence calibration, and gradient schedule.

Its supervised output is an action-update vector: the direction in which a noisy action estimate should move toward the target action. For a training pair ( o t , o t + i ) (o_{t},o_{t+i}) , let 𝐚 ~ t , t + i \tilde{\mathbf{a}}_{t,t+i} denote the ground-truth camera-space action defined in Appendix B . sections.heading: Masked and confidence-weighted errors.
sections.text: The implementation uses weighted robust errors for the two objectives. For prediction 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , target 𝐲 \mathbf{y} , and nonnegative coordinate weights 𝐰 \mathbf{w} , we compute ℛ ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 , 𝐰 ) = ∑ j w j ​ ( 1 + ( x j − y j ) 2 − 1 ) ∑ j w j , \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y};\mathbf{w})=\frac{\sum_{j}w_{j}\left(\sqrt{1+(x_{j}-y_{j})^{2}}-1\right)}{\sum_{j}w_{j}}, (22) over samples with nonzero total weight. Samples without valid supervised coordinates are omitted. The matching weights combine supervision validity, coordinate selection, and offline confidence calibrated on recorded transitions. The GT weights additionally account for the teacher’s reliability on the corresponding recorded image pair. Coordinates on which the teacher has a larger error against the ground-truth flow target receive less weight in the GT objective. These weights are held fixed when differentiating with respect to generated images. The projected start coordinates remain part of AoE’s action representation and receive zero direct auxiliary weight. Using these weights, the implemented action-flow objectives are ℒ match rob \displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{rob}}_{\mathrm{match}} = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ℛ ⁡ ( f ϕ ​ ( o t , o ^ t + i ) , f ϕ ​ ( o t , o t + i ) , 𝐰 match ) ] , \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{R}\left(f_{\phi}(o_{t},\hat{o}_{t+i}),f_{\phi}(o_{t},o_{t+i});\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{match}}\right)\right], (23) ℒ GT rob \displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{rob}}_{\mathrm{GT}} = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ℛ ⁡ ( f ϕ ​ ( o t , o ^ t + i ) , 𝐯 t , i ⋆ , 𝐰 GT ) ] . \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{R}\left(f_{\phi}(o_{t},\hat{o}_{t+i}),\mathbf{v}^{\star}_{t,i};\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{GT}}\right)\right]. To provide a direct image-space anchor, we supplement the matching objective with a weak reconstruction term around the ground-truth gripper locations. This ROI term uses Gaussian spatial weights and a Charbonnier reconstruction error. It is included as an implementation-level stabilizer alongside the matching loss.

sections.heading: Gradient propagation and training.
sections.text: Generated future frames are decoded differentiably before being passed to AoE. AoE and the video decoder retain frozen parameters, while gradients through their inputs update the world model. The two auxiliary objectives are averaged over the supervised future frames and added to the native training objective. For WAMs, the native action objective is retained, and the auxiliary gradients reach the video branch and shared parameters. Evaluation follows the original action inference path.

sections.heading: Appendix F Training and Evaluation Details
sections.text: This appendix summarizes the data sources, pretraining configuration, world-model settings, replay protocol, and downstream WAM training configurations used in our experiments. Unless otherwise specified, all settings are kept fixed across the corresponding comparisons. We separate training provenance from evaluation protocol because the two serve different purposes in the study. The former determines what information a model can use to learn a representation, while the latter determines whether the same representation transfers when task identities, object arrangements, or rendering conditions change. Each table therefore records the source data and optimization choices first, followed by the protocol that is held fixed in the corresponding comparison. The same convention applies to AoE. A checkpoint is trained once in the canonical-action stage and then reused as a frozen inverse-dynamics model in evaluation and VITA training. Freezing the checkpoint makes the teacher interface identical across world models and WAMs, so differences between rows can be attributed to the image source or the auxiliary objective rather than to a changing action translator. Whenever a table reports replay, the replay environment and initial state are synchronized with the image pair supplied to AoE.

sections.heading: F.1 Canonical-Action Pretraining
sections.text: AoE is initialized through canonical-action pretraining on a large-scale robot corpus. The corpus contains 9,637 9{,}637 hours of robot interaction data. The authoritative corpus total is reported in Table 9 ; Table 9 reports the duration and source type of each constituent dataset. The canonical-action model is trained on 64 H800 GPUs using BF16 precision. We use a global batch size of 1,024 and train for 600K optimization steps. Episodes are sampled with a mixing temperature of 1.0, and each episode provides 1,536 image pairs for canonical-action learning. The remaining optimization and regularization settings are listed in Table 10 . Validation is performed on held-out data from DROID, AgibotWorld, and LET. These validation streams are used for checkpoint selection and calibration only; they do not provide examples from the held-out downstream tasks used in the cross-task tests. The pretraining stage therefore supplies a common camera-space action interface before any target benchmark is introduced. Each training pair is formed from observations that share the same episode context but are separated by a valid interaction interval. Pair sampling preserves the endpoint relation that AoE must recover, while state dropout prevents the model from relying on a single proprioceptive cue when the visual transition already determines the motion. sections.heading: VITA gains across IDM evaluators.
sections.text: Comparing Table 24 with Table 22 , VITA increases LIBERO-Plus execution success from 0.5% to 29.9% with AoE, from 1.8% to 26.8% with J-IDM, and from 0.9% to 30.8% with DreamGen-IDM. These correspond to improvements of approximately 29.4, 25.0, and 29.9 percentage points, respectively. We compare each evaluator against its own no-VITA baseline; the Overall values should not be interpreted as a ranking across IDMs because their category coverage differs. The improvements with J-IDM and DreamGen-IDM show that the benefit of VITA is not restricted to action recovery by its AoE teacher. Nevertheless, VITA-supervised futures remain below the recorded-video replay reference for each evaluator, leaving a residual gap between generated and recorded visual transitions. The RoboTwin results in Table 22 provide complementary evidence that VITA-supervised futures remain executable under alternative action-recovery interfaces. J-IDM achieves 65.5%/66.7% on Easy/Hard, and DreamGen-IDM achieves 61.9%/57.8%, compared with 59.6%/40.4% for AoE. Since J-IDM and DreamGen-IDM are trained in-distribution for these evaluations, their results should not be interpreted as zero-shot cross-task generalization by the IDMs themselves. Rather, the LIBERO-Plus comparisons demonstrate improvements under independently trained evaluators, while the RoboTwin results confirm that the VITA-supervised futures support execution beyond the teacher’s own action-recovery interface. Together, these controls provide evidence that VITA improves executable visual information rather than merely matching AoE-specific responses.

Chen Zhao Affiliation: Key Laboratory of Data Engineering and KnowledgeEngineering, MOE, China Email: <2021201645@ruc.edu.cn Zipeng Ye Email: zhang-jing>@ruc.edu.cn Yihan Lin Affiliation: Key Laboratory of Data Engineering and KnowledgeEngineering, MOE, China Yuchen Xie Jing Zhang Affiliation: Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Affiliation: Meituan, Beijing 100102, China Abstract Cross-task generalization remains difficult for world action models (WAMs), even when their predicted futures depict plausible manipulation. This gap can be attributed directly: we make this gap directly testable by decoupling a WAM into a world model and an inverse-dynamics model (IDM), then holding the IDM fixed while replacing the source of future images. We introduce Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE), a camera-space inverse-dynamics model pretrained on large-scale robot data, which provides this recovery interface for different future sources across tasks and environments. Through it, we find that actions recovered from recorded futures of unseen tasks execute almost as well as replayed demonstrations, whereas futures predicted by world models collapse across benchmarks. The failures are not generic: they concentrate on the gripper and interaction geometry while generation capacity is spent on task-irrelevant background. This diagnosis suggests that supervision should target exactly these regions. We therefore introduce the vision-to-action (VITA) loss, which passes generated futures through the frozen AoE and penalizes discrepancies in the recovered actions, redirecting generation toward action-relevant detail. Across two world models and three manipulation benchmarks, this simple change raises the execution success of generated futures from near zero to 47.0%. The same loss also transfers to WAMs and yields consistent gains in native control. $\ast$ $\ast$ footnotetext: Equal contribution. $\dagger$ $\dagger$ footnotetext: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction World action models (WAMs) offer a compelling premise for embodied tasks: use the generalization capabilities of world models (WMs) to imagine future scenes, then condition an action head on the latent representations of those imagined futures to generate actions ( Li et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . This approach achieves strong performance on in-distribution tasks and under modest distribution shifts, yet falls substantially behind in more challenging settings, such as generalization across environments or tasks. This gap is often attributed to the difficulty of predicting 3D poses or to action heads that are tightly coupled to the environment encountered during training. Recent studies have also identified problems in world model predictions of robotic scenes, including physically implausible behavior and 2D-like flat appearance ( Shang et al., 2026 ; Co et al., 2026 ) . However, these analyses remain confined to 2D future videos that cannot be executed directly, leaving the impact of world model predictions on downstream cross-task generalization unquantified. Evaluating these videos through an inverse dynamics model (IDM) can also be inconclusive: exposure to trajectories from downstream environments during training may allow the IDM to compensate for distorted predictions, obscuring whether the predicted futures themselves support execution. To better evaluate the executability of future videos predicted by world models, we develop Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE). Pretrained on 9,637h of robot data, AoE uses camera-space representation to decouple action prediction from downstream environments. With little data from a downstream environment, AoE translates 2D gripper displacements and depth changes into executable poses. Figure 1: Overview of Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE) . Trained on 9,637 hours of robot image–action pairs, AoE infers the action between any two frames, serving as a bridge from video to action. Left: AoE enables evaluation of WMs: dreamed task completions in unseen environments are decoded into executable actions and assessed in the real environment. Right: The proposed vision-to-action (VITA) loss further improves the world (action) model by aligning actions recorded and inferred from dreamed and recorded videos. This enables interactive execution beyond the environments seen during pretraining, while keeping action trajectories out of training. On the same unseen benchmarks, we observe a substantial gap between recorded videos and world model predictions: actions recovered from recorded videos approach the success rate of replaying recorded actions, whereas those recovered from predicted future videos perform poorly. 2D flat appearance, physically implausible pose, and hallucinated scene substantially degrade the quality of the recovered poses ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Mi et al., 2026 ) . To address this limitation, we introduce the vision-to-action (VITA) loss, which uses AoE as a frozen supervisor to guide world models toward preserving the visual details needed for physically accurate gripper motion. We pass predicted future videos through AoE and use discrepancies of action-space representation to supervise action-relevant visual details ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . AoE’s sensitivity to gripper motion directs this supervision toward regions that matter for downstream execution ( Wi et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2020 ) . Gradients propagate through AoE to the world model while AoE itself remains frozen. VITA is natively suitable for world action model training to supervise predicted visual futures, allowing action-grounded visual supervision to shape the representations used for native action prediction. This supervision is applied during training and does not require the model to explicitly generate future images during execution. Our experiments examine three aspects of this approach. First, we use AoE to evaluate the cross-task executability of future videos generated by existing world models. Comparing generated futures with recorded videos reveals a substantial execution gap, highlighting a limitation in the transfer of world-model predictions to unseen tasks. Second, we evaluate VITA in both world models and world action models. VITA substantially improves the execution success of actions recovered from generated futures and improves native action prediction in LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026a ) and FastWAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , with particularly pronounced gains under distribution shifts ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Zhen et al., 2026 ) . FastWAM benefits even though it does not explicitly generate future images during inference. Third, we study how scaling AoE’s pretraining data affects its roles as both an evaluator and a supervisor. Larger-scale pretraining improves action recovery on unseen tasks and yields stronger downstream performance when the frozen AoE is used for VITA supervision. Our contributions are threefold: (1) we introduce AoE, an inverse dynamics model that uses the camera-space action representation to support zero-shot cross-task generalization; (2) we propose VITA, an action-grounded loss that uses frozen AoE supervision to guide both WMs and WAMs to preserve visual details needed for executable 3D pose changes; and (3) we demonstrate that VITA raises the cross-task execution success of world-model-generated futures from near zero to 47.0% and improves native action generation in WAMs under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution. 2 Preliminaries Forward and inverse dynamics. Let o t o_{t} denote the robot’s observation at time t t , a t a_{t} its action, and ℓ \ell a language instruction specifying the task. A forward dynamics model (FDM) predicts the consequences of an action. Written in observation space, its prediction takes the form o ^ t + 1 = ℱ θ ​ ( o t , a t ) , \hat{o}_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}_{	heta}(o_{t},a_{t}), (1) where θ 	heta denotes the model parameters and o ^ t + 1 \hat{o}_{t+1} is the predicted next observation. An inverse dynamics model (IDM) infers an action consistent with an observed transition: a ^ t = 𝒟 ϕ ​ ( o t , o t + 1 ) , \hat{a}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{\phi}(o_{t},o_{t+1}), (2) where ϕ \phi denotes the IDM parameters. These two mappings connect actions and observations in complementary directions: forward dynamics predicts what an action will produce, while inverse dynamics recovers an action that could produce a given transition. Applied to selected frame pairs from a video, inverse dynamics provides a way to translate visual changes into robot actions. From world models to world action models. In embodied tasks, a world model provides the visual-prediction component of a policy. An instruction-conditioned world model predicts a task-directed future observation from the current observation and instruction. WAMs integrate this prediction process with action generation ( Li et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . In attention-based architectures, an action head reads internal visual features associated with the predicted future. We summarize this interface as h t = ℋ θ ​ ( o t , ℓ ) , a ^ t = 𝒜 ψ ​ ( o t , ℓ , h t ) , h_{t}=\mathcal{H}_{	heta}(o_{t},\ell),\qquad\hat{a}_{t}=\mathcal{A}_{\psi}(o_{t},\ell,h_{t}), (3) where h t h_{t} denotes the latent features associated with future prediction, ℋ θ \mathcal{H}_{	heta} denotes their computation within the world model, and 𝒜 ψ \mathcal{A}_{\psi} is the action head. Attention allows the action head to access h t h_{t} during action prediction. Training this coupled system on downstream data ties the visual features to the action head that consumes them. Future imagination therefore influences control through an internal representation, and task success reflects the behavior of the combined system. This makes it difficult to directly assess how the predicted visual future itself supports execution on unseen tasks. We introduce an explicit image-space interface between future prediction and action recovery: o ^ t + 1 = 𝒲 θ ​ ( o t , ℓ ) , a ^ t = 𝒟 ϕ ​ ( o t , o ^ t + 1 ) , \hat{o}_{t+1}=\mathcal{W}_{	heta}(o_{t},\ell),\qquad\hat{a}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{\phi}(o_{t},\hat{o}_{t+1}), (4) where 𝒲 θ \mathcal{W}_{	heta} is the instruction-conditioned world model and 𝒟 ϕ \mathcal{D}_{\phi} is an independently pretrained IDM. We first evaluate the IDM on recorded transitions from unseen tasks. We then replace the recorded future observations with world-model predictions while keeping the IDM frozen. This shared action-recovery interface allows us to evaluate IDM transfer and the executability of generated futures separately under the same execution protocol. 3 Method We introduce AoE, an inverse dynamics model pretrained on 9,637 hours of robot image–action pairs, and use it as a frozen interface for evaluating and improving WMs and WAMs for embodied tasks. Section 3.1 presents AoE’s overview and our protocol for evaluating the executability of future videos generated for unseen tasks. Section 3.2 introduces the AoE-based vision-to-action (VITA) loss and its integration into world-model and WAM training. Section 3.3 analyzes how this loss guides future prediction and improves downstream execution. Figure 2: Cross-task generalization evaluation and the VITA loss. Left: Future videos generated by the WM in unseen environments are fed into AoE frame-by-frame to obtain camera-space representations, which are translated into 3D poses and executed in the real environment for evaluation. Middle: Dreamed future frames are decoded by AoE into actions, and the WM is updated by minimizing their discrepancies against actions inferred from recorded videos as well as the ground-truth actions. Right: The vision-to-action loss is transferred to WAM. By encouraging the future video to focus on task-critical regions, the native action generation of WAM is improved under cross-task generalization. 3.1 Camera-Space Inverse Dynamics for Cross-Task Evaluation An IDM infers actions that connect a current observation o t o_{t} to a future observation o t + i o_{t+i} . A growing body of work evaluates world models in embodied scenarios. WorldArena jointly scores perceptual quality and functional utility, revealing a persistent gap between visual fidelity and embodied usefulness ( Shang et al., 2026 ) . KineBench grounds generated videos kinematically, extracting end-effector poses from individual frames for closed-loop execution and trajectory-level analysis ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , and WorldSimProbe issues controlled simulator queries to test action realization and interaction grounding ( Co et al., 2026 ) . Despite this progress, existing evaluations remain confined to imagination: they score the generated videos themselves, or execute them only through extractors tied to their training environments, leaving unquantified whether a predicted future can be carried into an unseen environment and actually executed ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . We therefore use dataset-image and recorded-action replay to calibrate IDM transfer, and hold the pretrained IDM fixed across visual-source replacements, human judgments, and local geometric interventions. Video and inverse-dynamics priors for control. DreamGen converts generated videos into neural trajectories for policy training ( Jang et al., 2025 ) . LingBot-VA couples causal video modeling with action prediction ( Li et al., 2026a ) , while Fast-WAM studies video co-training under several inference interfaces ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) . VERA combines video planning with a Jacobian-based inverse dynamics model ( Li et al., 2026b ) . GE-Act 2.0 separately pretrains a visual planner and IDM, then jointly optimizes them through generated future states using action flow matching and compatibility-based selection ( AgiBot Research Team et al., 2026 ) . These approaches establish visual prediction and inverse dynamics as complementary components of robot learning. We evaluate a pretrained, frozen camera-space IDM through dataset-image replay on held-out tasks and transfer its action knowledge into future-image supervision. 6 Conclusion Pretrained inverse dynamics provides a common action model for evaluating and supervising visual futures. We introduce AoE, an inverse-dynamics model built on a camera-projection action representation with zero-shot cross-task generalization, through which world-model futures are carried from video into interactive execution in the environment. Building on this interface, we further propose the VITA loss, which substantially improves the cross-task generalization of world models. We also extend VITA to world action models, obtaining consistent gains across multiple architectures and evaluation environments. Constrained by the camera-projection representation, AoE cannot handle tasks where the gripper leaves the camera view for extended periods or the camera is severely occluded, and would raise additional safety concerns in real-robot evaluation; we expect these limitations to be addressed in combination with future work on active exploration.
